claims.text: A higher density of low-coordinated defect sites promotes the formation of synergistic adjacent active centers in PGM-based nanoscale ethanol-oxidation catalysts.
The synergistic adjacent active centers facilitate multistep proton-electron transfer during ethanol oxidation.
Increasing defect density reduces poisoning by intermediates such as CO.
A calibrated annealing or etching treatment can increase surface-defect density without changing the catalyst's overall composition.
Surface defects produce low-coordinated atomic sites with altered local electronic states.
Increasing defect density shifts the catalyst's d-band center.
Defect sites modify the binding energies of key ethanol-oxidation intermediates and thereby facilitate ethanol activation and dehydrogenation.
Defect sites lower the activation energy associated with the 12-electron and 12-proton ethanol-oxidation process.
Defect-rich surfaces can improve intermediate removal or open alternative oxidation pathways.
Increasing defect density will increase ethanol-oxidation current density at a fixed overpotential.
Increasing defect density will reduce deactivation and improve durability during ethanol oxidation.
The proposed benefit applies when ethanol oxidation is rate-limited by intermediate binding and dehydrogenation.
The defect-related benefit may diminish or reverse at very high temperatures or in aggressive acidic environments.
Extreme operating conditions can corrode the catalyst or restructure its defect sites.
An excessively high defect density may create a trade-off between catalytic activity and long-term structural stability.
The optimal defect density is not known precisely.
The defect-density hypothesis can be tested by comparing composition-matched, lower-defect and defect-enhanced catalysts under identical electrochemical conditions.
A lack of statistically significant improvement in activity and durability, or worsened performance, would falsify the proposed beneficial effect of increased defect density.
